name: Carolina Blue
lede: Carolina Blue is a pale, greyed sky blue known today as the color of the University of North Carolina at Chapel Hill, though a swatch close to it already sat in a color atlas the same year the name is first recorded in our sources.

sections.title: A university blue, or an older swatch
sections.body:
Wikipedia credits the University of North Carolina at Chapel Hill as this color's namesake, tying it to the school's light blue athletic color; that attribution is the only record we have of the naming itself [1]. Robert Ridgway's 1912 nomenclature for naturalists already carries a very close hue on plate VIII, and the ISCC-NBS system later classified this chip as a brilliant blue, about 3.3 units from that block's reference color [2]. Whether Ridgway's swatch and the university's blue share any real history, or are simply the same pale blue arrived at twice, is not something our sources settle [1][2].

The nearest named colors on file are [[iceberg]] and [[blue-grey]], at [[columbia-blue|Columbia Blue]] sits in the same family of pale institutional blues, lighter and slightly greyer than this one, and [[powder-blue|Powder Blue]] and [[sky-blue|Sky Blue]] sit further out among its more saturated relatives [2].

sections.title: Field notes
sections.body:
Our archive finds a close match to this blue in 25 of 23,781 paintings, about 0.11 percent, and in 13 by the stricter within-painting measure, which makes it rarer than 65 percent of the named colors we track [3]. Inside those paintings it most often sits as an accent, 46 percent of the 13, rather than a dominant field of color [3]. It is most over-represented in paintings from France, at 2.8 times the expected rate, and peaks in paintings from the 1800s, at 1.1 times expected [3].

The earliest match in our archive is a 1485 painting attributed to Martin Bernat, with the latest dated match from 1907, 20 paintings in all, a floor and not a first, since the archive's early centuries are thin [3]. That earliest match is 427 years before the name's own earliest record in our sources, 1912: it is a look-alike hue in an aged photograph, not evidence that the named color existed that early [2][3]. These are photographs of aged, varnished paintings, read as screen colors, not pigment identifications[3].

questions.answer: An aged photograph happens to match the hue, not proof the color existed by that name

openers: Carolina Blue is named for a university, but a near-identical hue already sat in a 1912 color atlas.
In our archive, this blue shows up in a painting from 1485 -- centuries before the name existed, by coincidence of hue.

issues: Relation between Ridgway's 1912 swatch and the university naming is not documented in our sources; both left hedged.
